did.unittitle: Brooklyn Historical Society Civil War collection

physdesc.extent: in two manuscript boxes, one flat box and one flat file folder.

did.abstract: Various Civil War materials from New York and the Eastern United States, ranging from Confederate military records to ephemeral printed material. The collection includes hospital records, roll books and registers, muster rolls, military orders, scrapbooks, broadsides, photographs and ephemera.
did.langmaterial: Materials primarily in English, with some broadsides in German.

acqinfo.head: Immediate Source of Acquisition
acqinfo.p: Source and date of acquisition for the majority of the collection is unknown. The collection was accessioned in 1977. Portions of the collection may be the gift of Caroline Griswold, April 1864, having been picked up by one of her nephews in the County Clerk's Office in Culpepper, VA. Additional acquisition information is noted at the file level when known.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The material is arranged into four series by source or type. Series 1 consists of material mostly relating to Andersonville Prison Hospital and collected by E.P. Hopkins. The other materials in the series were housed with the Andersonville materials under the same accession number and are presumed to belong together. The series is arranged chronologically. Series 2 includes four scrapbooks, two of which were compiled by George R. Howell, arranged chronologically. Series 3 consists of various other materials, some of which were found in collection, also arranged chronologically. Finally, Series 4 consists of found-in-collection photographs.

bioghist.head: Historical note
bioghist.p: Andersonville Prison Hospital, represented in the collection through hospital records and registers, was located in southwest Georgia and operated for 15 months between 1864 and 1865. The site was used by the Confederate Army as a prisoner-of-war camp for captured Union soldiers. At the time of its closure, almost 13,000 Union soldiers had died at Andersonville. The records in this collection were collected by E.P. Hopkins, a captured Ohio soldier who worked as a Steward in the prison hospital. In the autumn of 1864, after the Battle of Atlanta, all the prisoners who were well enough to be moved were sent to Florence Stockade (near Florence, South Carolina) and Camp Lawton (near Millen, Georgia). From Millen, prisoners were transported by rail to the port of Savannah. This collection includes documents relating to both Millen and Savannah as well.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: Originally minimally processed to the collection level, this collection was reprocessed and the finding aid revised by Dee Bowers in November 2026. As the original accession, 1977.200, had little accession documentation and seemed already to be a composite of two or more acquisitions, the collection, which had been titled simply "Civil War collection," was combined with related unaccessioned material that had been found in collection, renamed "Brooklyn Historical Society Civil War collection," and renumbered ARC.326 to reflect its composite nature.

relatedmaterial.head: Related Materials
relatedmaterial.p: Many other Civil War materials are listed in CBH's research guide on the subject.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This collection contains a variety of materials from New York and the Eastern United States, ranging from Confederate military records to ephemeral printed material. Document types in the collection include hospital records, roll books, registers, muster rolls, military orders, scrapbooks, broadsides, and ephemera.

The bulk of military records in the collection are records from the Andersonville Prison Hospital in Georgia. These records document the work of the hospital and doctors during the summer of 1864 with daily hospital admission lists, death registers, roll books, hospital registers, and daily medical officer reports. Registers from Andersonville list patient name, rank, company, and regiment. Other items related to the Confederate Army include a report on the Battle of Fair Oaks in 1862, and a muster roll of the 36th North Carolina Infantry Regiment, Company C, listing name, rank, and enlistment dates of soldiers in the company.

Broadsides and ephemera cover events and organizations local to Brooklyn, New York City, Queens, and Long Island from the early 19th century to the Civil War era. The broadsides provide discussion of local, regional, and national issues, such as drafts, slavery, temperance, elections, and political platforms, and represent organizations such as the National Freedman's Relief Association, the War Fund Committee of Brooklyn, and the Suffolk County Sabbath School Association. A small number of broadsides related to the election of 1864 are written in German. Printed ephemera includes promotional material for two Brooklyn newspapers, the Brooklyn Evening Star and the Brooklyn Daily Union. The collection also contains four scrapbooks--three with pro-Union envelopes and printed ephemera, two of which were compiled by George R. Howell, and one with political cartoons from the election of 1864.

Additionally, the collection includes materials from the 159th Regiment New York State Volunteers Veterans' Association as well as many cartes-de-visite photographs of Civil War soldiers and notable Civil War era figures.

userestrict.head: Conditions Governing Use
userestrict.p: The materials in this collection are in the public domain. While many items at the Center for Brooklyn History are unrestricted, we do not own reproduction rights to all materials. Be aware of the several kinds of rights that might apply: copyright, licensing and trademarks. The researcher assumes all responsibility for copyright questions.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Edwin P. Hopkins was born in Zanesville, Muskingum County, OH in 1841 or 1842. He enlisted in the 1st Ohio Volunteer Light Artillery Regiment, Battery H on October 27, 1861. He was captured on November 27, 1863 during the Mine Run Campaign and imprisoned in Richmond, VA. In March 1864 he was transferred to Andersonville and appointed Steward in charge of the 1st division of the camp hospital, which was divided into four divisions. He was released in November 1864 and as of May 1865 was living in Toledo, Ohio. Andersonville Prison, officially named Camp Sumter and located in Andersonville, GA, was active from February 1864 until the end of the Civil War in April 1865 and was one of the largest Confederate prisoner of war camps. The camp covered 26.5 acres and held up to 32,000 prisoners during the height of its use. Over the fifteen months it was in operation almost 13,000 prisoners died as a result of the extremely poor living conditions created by overcrowding and a scarcity of supplies of medicine, food, clothing and shelter.

custodhist.head: Custodial History
custodhist.p: Edwin Hopkins collected the Andersonville materials in the first series while a prisoner at Andersonville. The records are original documents that were consolidated into reports by the surgeon in charge of each division and then submitted to the Chief Surgeon. Afterwards the originals were sent back to the Steward to be discarded. Hopkins, however, did not discard them and instead secreted them away and took them with him when he left Andersonville in November 1864. Nothing is known of how they came to be at the Brooklyn Historical Society.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: At the time of processing, the original hardcover scrapbook was in poor condition. As the materials within it were either loose or confined to a small number of pages, with the rest of the volume blank, the archivist removed the contents and pages and discarded the empty pages, covers, and spine.
